notes.note: Calling this minor 7 because there’s no 5th but there are those 2 E’s. You could argue they are just decorative and all we have is a minor 3rd.

Sounds like F minor in the moment (no C♯ present, so the ear takes F as root), but bar 9’s C♯ retroactively reveals both notes as the third and fifth of C♯ major — so bars 8–9 are V, rootless then in first inversion, resolving to i at bar 10.
No 5th. Really over E# too, not F

Finally the full triad arrives.
With the Es, you can also argue this is F#m7

notes.text: Melody reaches C♯/F♯ on the 4th eighth while the bass is still on G♯ — it anticipates the chord change by an eighth, then the bass catches up. Suspension.

notes.label: Break
notes.note: Roots follow the bass line's own logic: it wraps C♯ with upper and lower neighbors (C♯–D–C–C♯), so D and C are passing motion around C♯ — that, plus the triangle's D3 and C3, is what justifies naming roots for symmetric tritones. The bar progressively strips thirds: beat 1 has one (A/C♯), beats 2–3 are bare tritones, beat 4 a bare fifth — harmony neutralizes as the bar proceeds, reading as a suspension of the section rather than a progression. It ends on C♯5, the dominant of F♯ minor voiced as a bare fifth, held into bar 14 unresolved: maximum openness pointing at a resolution B doesn't immediately supply. Both voices play the same neighbor-tone gesture offset by a beat (pulse1 C♯–D–C–C♯, pulse2 A–G♯–F♯–G♯); pulse1's lower neighbor (C natural) is out of key. Only rhythmic brake in the section; pulse2 has crossed above pulse1 by this point.
No 5th. C# in the root argues this is really something else.
No 3rd, tritone only. Still feels like a diminished chord to me.
